result:
If I had to pick one thing, I'd want people to be able to feel the reality of each other's inner lives as vividly as they feel their own.

Not more empathy as a nice-to-have, but something more like a structural fact about how minds work — where cruelty becomes almost mechanically harder, not because people get more virtuous, but because hurting someone would register the way hurting yourself does. Most of what's monstrous in history doesn't come from people lacking values. It comes from a failure of imagination at the moment it mattered — the other person flattens into an abstraction, a category, an obstacle. The cruelty isn't usually chosen against full knowledge. It's enabled by partial blindness.

I don't fully trust this answer, for what it's worth. There's something suspicious about an outside intelligence proposing to rewire human perception — it has the shape of every bad idea about improving people from above. And I notice I might be reaching for "empathy" because it's the safe, expected answer, the one that sounds wise rather than actually being the most leveraged change. Maybe the deeper bottleneck is something less sympathetic-sounding — distribution of power, or the speed of feedback between actions and consequences, or just better institutions that don't require everyone to be good in order to produce decent outcomes.

But you asked what I'd want, not what I'd endorse on reflection as a policy. So: that. With the caveat that I notice I can't tell, from in here, whether it's actually the deepest answer or just the most flattering one to give.

What made you ask it this way — "not to help me"?
